papers.title: Keeping Inference in the Radio: Design and Measurement of a Spiking Accelerator for mmWave ISAC Activity Recognition
authors: Anthony S\'anchez, Rafael Ruiz, Jos\'e A. Belloch, Jes\'us O. Lacruz, Joerg Widmer
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.37480v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication allows wireless networks to recognize human activity from the channel estimates that the receiver computes anyway. The inference, however, runs on the general-purpose processors of the base station, access point or handset, which are the first components a device switches off to save energy. Always-on sensing therefore requires a classifier that is small enough to remain powered while the rest of the system sleeps. We investigate whether Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) can provide such a classifier. papers.title: Hardware-Matched Spiking Neural Networks for Real-Time Purkinje Cell Spike Classification
authors: Arooba Farhan, Afsah Syed, Muhammad Fahd Ibrahim Bhatti, Muhammad Areeb Khalid Kidwai, Muhammad Ahsan Salar Khan, Vincenzo Romano, Muhammad Ali Siddiqi
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.37104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distinguishing Purkinje cell (PC) simple spikes (SSs) from complex spikes (CSs) is key to studying cerebellar function. PC recordings commonly rely on wired headstages, whose tethers restrict natural movement in freely behaving animals. Untethered headstages remove this constraint, but cannot continuously transmit raw recordings within their power budgets, making on-headstage spike classification an attractive form of compression, provided it runs accurately in real time on constrained hardware. papers.title: Kernel Performance Engineering under Physical Non-Idealities
authors: Supun Kuruppu, Pranav Dangi, Wei Li, Zhenyu Bai, Tulika Mitra
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.37466v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physical non-idealities in integrated circuit (IC) design and fabrication are concealed by conventional hardware abstractions, yet they can limit kernel performance and obscure optimization opportunities. Using distributed shared memory (DSMEM) on NVIDIA H100 GPUs as a case study, we show how floorsweeping restricts hardware resources available for clustered execution, potentially offsetting the benefits of reduced data movement enabled by DSMEM. Guided by these insights, we develop a wave-aware clustering strategy that accounts for these resource constraints to improve kernel performance. papers.title: RV565: Cross-Layer Co-Design for Frame-Independent Video Playback on MicroPython-Class ESP32-S3 Systems
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.35935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video on SPI-attached microcontroller displays is limited less by decoding than by where each byte lives and which stages run serially. We present RV565, a decode framework for frame-independent video whose decoded representation is the panel's native RGB565 format, and evaluate it on an ESP32-S3 with two ten-second windows of an openly licensed film. A serial path - inflate, then scale into internal-memory stripes overlapped with SPI direct-memory-access (DMA) transfers - meets the 41.7 ms deadline on the lighter window but misses all 7,200 frames of the heavier one.
